title: NICODEMUS KNEW RELIGION — JESUS TOLD HIM HE STILL NEEDED TO BE BORN AGAIN
paragraphs: NICODEMUS KNEW RELIGION — JESUS TOLD HIM HE STILL NEEDED TO BE BORN AGAIN

He knew Scripture. He respected God. He had status, morality, theology, and religion. Then Jesus looked at this respected religious man and told him, in effect: none of that can give you the life only God can give.
There is something unsettling about Nicodemus coming to Jesus at night.
Not because darkness automatically means cowardice. John does not explicitly tell us why he chose that hour, so we should be careful not to accuse him of motives Scripture does not name.
But John does tell us it was night.
And somehow, that detail stays with you.
A respected man walking through darkened streets toward Jesus.
A teacher going to meet the Teacher.
A religious leader carrying questions his religion had not answered.
A man who probably appeared spiritually secure to almost everyone around him… about to discover that being surrounded by the things of God is not the same as possessing the life of God.
Maybe that is why his story can feel frighteningly personal.
Because some of us know how to look Christian.
We know when to say, “Amen.”
We know worship songs.
We know Bible verses.
We know church language.
We know what Christians are supposed to post, what Christians are supposed to condemn, and what Christians are supposed to say when someone asks how we are doing.
We may have been baptized.
We may serve.
We may give.
We may preach.
We may defend Christian doctrine online.
We may have spent decades around Christianity.
And still there is one question that can strip away every religious credential we have collected:
Have I actually been born again?
Nicodemus was not introduced as a pagan mocking God.
He was a Pharisee.
He was also called “a ruler of the Jews” (John 3:1). Jesus later referred to him as “the teacher of Israel” (John 3:10), language suggesting that Nicodemus was a recognized religious teacher.
This was not a spiritually indifferent man wandering accidentally into a conversation about God.
This was Nicodemus.
Religious.
Educated.
Respected.
Knowledgeable.
And he began respectfully:
“Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher come from God…”
But Jesus did something extraordinary.
He did not allow the conversation to remain at the level of admiration.
Nicodemus wanted to talk about who Jesus appeared to be.
Jesus went straight to what Nicodemus needed to become.
“Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.” (John 3:3)
The Greek deserves our attention.
Jesus says:
ἐὰν μή τις γεννηθῇ ἄνωθεν
ean mē tis gennēthē anōthen
The crucial word is ἄνωθεν — anōthen.
It can carry the sense of “again” and also “from above.”
That makes the encounter even richer.
Nicodemus hears Jesus and immediately thinks in terms of another physical birth:
“How can a man be born when he is old?”
But Jesus is speaking about something no human being can manufacture.
Birth from above.
Life originating in God.
Not religious renovation.
Not behavioral cosmetics.
Not becoming a slightly nicer version of the old person.
New life.
That distinction destroys one of Christianity's most dangerous counterfeits: the assumption that proximity to Christian things is the same as regeneration.
It is not.
You can learn Christian vocabulary without receiving a new heart.
You can modify behavior while secretly loving the same darkness.
You can become more religious without becoming more surrendered.
You can know facts about Jesus without belonging to Jesus.
You can spend years cleaning the outside while hiding what is dying inside.
Nicodemus had religion.
Jesus told him he needed birth.
And there is an enormous difference between the two.
Religion can teach the old person how to behave.
Only God can give the sinner new life.
This was not an entirely foreign concept to Israel's Scriptures.
God had already promised through Ezekiel:
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.” (Ezekiel 36:26)
The Hebrew phrase for “new heart” is:
לֵב חָדָשׁ — lev chadash
A new heart.
God continues by promising to remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh, and then says:
“I will put my Spirit within you…” (Ezekiel 36:27)
This is not humanity climbing its way toward God.
This is God doing what humanity cannot do for itself.
That is why Jesus continues:
“Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” (John 3:5)

Christians have discussed the precise interpretation of “water and Spirit,” and faithful interpreters have not always agreed on every detail. But the wider context unmistakably emphasizes the necessity of the Spirit's work and the inability of natural human birth to produce spiritual life.
“That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.” (John 3:6)
Then Jesus gives Nicodemus an image he cannot control.
The wind.
“The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” (John 3:8)
In Greek, the word πνεῦμα — pneuma can mean spirit, wind, or breath, depending on context.
Jesus is showing Nicodemus that the new birth is not another religious achievement to place on a spiritual résumé.
You do not earn birth.
You receive life.
And maybe someone reading this has spent years trying to earn what only Christ can give.
You keep promising God you will do better.
Then you fail.
You feel filthy.
You withdraw.
You return.
You promise harder.
You survive for a few weeks.
Then the secret comes back.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The pride.
The affair nobody knows about.
The hatred.
The greed.
The unforgiveness.
The double life.
The desperate need to be admired.
The hidden habit.
The private compromise.
The prayerlessness beneath the public Christianity.
And eventually you become exhausted because you have been trying to decorate something Jesus came to put to death and make new.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave better.
He came to save sinners.
The Gospel is not self-improvement with Bible verses attached.
It is death and resurrection.
Sin exposed.
Judgment deserved.
Grace given.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Sinners forgiven.
Hearts transformed.
Lives surrendered.
And Jesus does not leave Nicodemus with an abstract lesson about spiritual rebirth.
He takes him somewhere darker.
To a serpent.
To a wilderness.
To a pole lifted before dying people.
“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up…” (John 3:14)
Nicodemus knew that story.
Israel had sinned against God in Numbers 21.
Judgment came.
People were dying.
God instructed Moses to make a bronze serpent and lift it on a pole. Those who had been bitten were not told to pretend they were healthy.
They were dying.
They had to look toward the provision God had given.
Jesus takes that ancient scene and points it toward Himself.
The Son of Man would be lifted up.
The respected teacher who came under the darkness of night was being told that his hope was not ultimately in his knowledge, reputation, religious position, ancestry, or morality.
His hope would be found in a crucified Messiah.
And then come words so famous that familiarity can make us forget how astonishing they are:
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.” (John 3:16)
Look at that word:
πιστεύων — pisteuōn
Believing.
Trusting.
Relying upon.
This is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
The demons can recognize truth about God (James 2:19).
Saving faith rests its hope in Christ.
You stop presenting your résumé to God as though your goodness can cancel your guilt.
You stop pretending your church attendance can atone for your sin.
You stop trusting the Christian image you constructed.
You come empty-handed to Jesus.
Because the scandal of grace is that the person who finally admits, “I cannot save myself,” is standing exactly where the Gospel begins to make sense.
Jesus continues:
“For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.” (John 3:17)
Do not misunderstand that verse as though Jesus teaches that sin does not matter.
The following verses speak plainly about judgment and humanity's love of darkness.
Jesus says:
“the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.” (John 3:19)
That hurts because darkness is not merely something “those people” love.
We know darkness.
We know what it feels like to delete evidence.
To hide a browser history.
To disguise motives.
To tell half the story.
To smile while dying inside.
To perform spirituality while protecting a secret room in the heart.
To want enough Jesus to quiet our conscience but not enough Jesus to surrender our throne.
But grace does something darkness hates.
Grace turns the light on.
Not so we can congratulate ourselves for being better than everybody else.
So we can finally stop hiding from the One who already knows.
This is where repentance becomes beautiful.
Biblical repentance is not paying God back for your sins.
You could never pay Him back.
It is not punishing yourself until you feel sufficiently miserable.
It is turning toward God in faith, agreeing with Him about sin, abandoning the illusion that sin can save or satisfy you, and throwing yourself upon the mercy offered in Christ.
You do not clean yourself enough to qualify for Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you cannot clean yourself.
And the cross destroys both despair and pride.
Despair says, “My sin is too great.”
The cross answers, “His grace is greater.”
Pride says, “I am good enough.”
The cross answers, “If you were good enough, the Son of God would not have needed to die for you.”
At Calvary, every mask falls.
There are no celebrities before the cross.
No religious VIP section.
No premium sinners.
No insignificant sinners.
No one enters the kingdom because his family was Christian.
No one enters because she knew theology.
No one enters because he had a ministry.
No one enters because she never committed the sins everybody could see.
We come through Christ.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” (John 14:6)
That means the question is no longer merely:
Do you believe in God?
Nicodemus believed in God.
The deeper question is:
Have you entrusted yourself to Jesus Christ?
Has your sin become something to confess rather than protect?
Has grace become your hope rather than your excuse?
Has Jesus become Lord rather than religious decoration?
Are you following Christ—or merely living close enough to Christianity to convince yourself that you are safe?
Do not answer quickly.
Some questions deserve silence.
Nicodemus disappears from the conversation in John 3 without John recording a dramatic conversion scene that night.
And that matters.
Scripture does not give us permission to invent one.
But Nicodemus appears again.
In John 7:50–52, when others are condemning Jesus, Nicodemus cautiously raises the question of whether their law judges a man without first hearing him.
Then comes John 19.
Jesus is dead.
The crowds have screamed.
The cross has done its terrible work.
The public spectacle has become a corpse.
And now identifying with Jesus is not fashionable.
There appears to be nothing earthly to gain.
Joseph of Arimathea comes for the body.
And John tells us:
“Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came…”
There it is again.
John remembers the night.
But this time Nicodemus is carrying something.
A mixture of myrrh and aloes.
About seventy-five pounds according to many modern English translations.
An extraordinarily large quantity of burial spices.
The man who once approached Jesus under cover of night is now participating in the burial of the crucified Christ.
We should still be careful. Scripture does not give us every detail of Nicodemus's inner spiritual journey, and we should not manufacture certainty where the Bible remains quiet.
But John wants us to remember him.
The man from the night is standing near the body of Jesus.
And perhaps that is where this story turns its gaze toward us.
Because eventually every borrowed Christianity must become personal.
Eventually your parents' faith cannot answer for you.
Your pastor cannot repent for you.
Your spouse cannot believe for you.
Your church cannot be born again for you.
Your theological knowledge cannot bleed for you.
Your reputation cannot rise from the grave for you.
You need Jesus.
Not the Christian aesthetic.
Not Christian culture.
Not inspirational quotations.
Not religious performance.
Jesus.
The crucified Son of God.
The risen King.
The Savior of sinners.
Maybe you have been hiding behind religion because admitting that you need saving feels humiliating.
But Christianity begins with that humiliation.
“I cannot save myself.”
And then comes the thunder of grace:
You do not have to.
Christ has done what you could never do.
He lived without sin.
He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
He bore judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose bodily from the dead.
The Gospel does not say your scandal was imaginary.
It says your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
It does not say sin is harmless.
It says Christ is mighty to save.
It does not say consequences always disappear.
It says condemnation does not belong to those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).
It does not say you become perfect overnight.
It says God begins a work of transformation that belongs to a genuinely new life.
This is from scandal to grace.
Not because God rewrites history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Because Jesus can rewrite what the scandal means for your future.
Peter's denial did not get the last word.
The thief's criminal past did not get the last word.
Paul's persecution of the church did not get the last word.
And your worst chapter does not have authority greater than Jesus Christ.
But grace is not permission to remain comfortably in darkness.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
The grace that pardons also transforms.
The Gospel does not merely rescue us from sin's penalty; it begins liberating us from sin's dominion and reshaping us into the likeness of Christ.
So maybe today you do not need another Christian post to admire.
Maybe you need to stop.
Put the phone down for a moment after you finish reading.
Tell God the truth.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary designed to sound impressive.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have been pretending, admit it.
If you have trusted religion instead of Christ, repent.
If you are exhausted from hiding, come into the light.
If you are unsure whether you understand the Gospel, open John's Gospel and begin reading Jesus for yourself.
And call upon Him.
Not because typing a phrase in a comment saves you.
It does not.
Jesus saves.
Not because sharing an article earns favor with God.
It does not.
Christ's finished work—not social-media activity—is the ground of salvation.
It does not. Scripture never gives us permission to place that burden on your conscience.
You glorify God through faith in Christ and a life increasingly surrendered to Him.

But if this message helped bring you back to Scripture, convicted you, reminded you of the Gospel, or reached you at a moment when you were quietly disappearing into darkness, you can help place that same truth in front of someone else.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that she is struggling.
Not because comments save souls.
Because sometimes confession breaks isolation, testimony strengthens another believer, and one person's willingness to say, “I need prayer,” gives someone else permission to stop pretending.

And if Gospel Warrior has become one of the places helping you stay close to Scripture, follow and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. The goal is not building an audience around us. The goal is continually pointing an audience beyond us—to Jesus Christ.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough posts to erase one sin.
You cannot donate enough money to make God owe you salvation.
That is exactly why the Gospel is so breathtaking.
The price you could never pay was met by Christ.
So support Gospel work because you love the One who saved you—not because anyone frightened you into believing that supporting a page could save your soul.
Share because someone needs the Gospel.
Tag because someone has a name.
Save because truth is worth returning to.
Follow because your soul needs more than an endless diet of noise.
But worship Jesus alone.
Because one night, a religious man walked toward Jesus carrying knowledge, reputation, morality, questions, and religion.
And Jesus looked beyond all of it.
He told him he needed life from above.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear too.
You do not need a more convincing mask.
You need Christ.
You do not need a cleaner hiding place.
You need the light.
You do not need another religious achievement.
You need grace.
And if you come to Jesus with nothing left to brag about and nothing left to hide, you will discover the heart of the Gospel:
The Savior already knew the chapter you were ashamed of when He called you to Himself.
Your darkest night does not have to become your final address—the Light is still calling your name.
